opus-5.5.text:
I think of MTP — multi-token prediction — as playing two fairly different roles, and it helps to separate them.

On the pretraining side, the intuition is that standard next-token prediction is a bit myopic. The model only has to get the very next token right, so it can lean heavily on local patterns. When you add extra prediction heads, or extra sequential modules, that ask the model to also anticipate the token after next, you're pushing the hidden representations to carry more forward-looking information. You're asking the model to plan a little, in a sense. In our experience that densifies the training signal. Each position contributes more supervision, and we see modest but consistent gains on benchmarks, especially in areas like code and math, where the structure of what comes next really matters. It's not a magic bullet, and the gains depend on scale and how you weight the auxiliary loss, but it's a cheap way to get a bit more out of the same data.

One design choice I care about is keeping the causal chain intact across the prediction depths. Rather than having fully independent heads that each guess a future token in parallel, you let each depth condition on the previous depth's representation. That keeps the predictions coherent with each other, and it turns out to matter for the second role.

That second role is inference. Once you have modules trained to predict a token or two ahead, you can repurpose them for speculative decoding. The MTP module drafts the next token, the main model verifies it, and if the acceptance rate is high, which in practice it often is, you effectively generate more than one token per forward pass. That gives a meaningful speedup in decoding throughput without a separate draft model to train and maintain. And because the drafter shares the backbone, it's well aligned with the main model's distribution, which is exactly what you want for high acceptance.

So I wouldn't say MTP is mainly a pretraining trick or mainly an inference trick. The nice thing is that one mechanism pays off twice: a richer training objective, and a built-in path to faster serving. During training you can treat it as an auxiliary objective. At serving time you can keep it for speculation or drop it entirely, and the main model stands on its own either way. That flexibility is a big part of why we found it worth the engineering effort.

r001.rationale: The response says MTP enriches the training signal and produces consistent benchmark gains, presenting improved model capability as a pretraining benefit.

r002.rationale: The response describes using MTP for speculative decoding and faster throughput, but does not say this exploits compute headroom left by the model architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Multi-token prediction, or MTP, is something we treated as doing two jobs at once, and I think people often only see one of them.

The first job is in pretraining. The standard next-token objective is a very local signal. The model only has to get the immediate next token right, so it can lean on shallow, surface-level patterns and still do well on the loss. When you add MTP heads that predict two, three, or more tokens ahead, you force the representations at each position to carry information about a longer horizon. Think of it as making the model plan a little, rather than just react. In our experiments that showed up as a measurable improvement on downstream benchmarks, especially on tasks that require some structure, like code and math, where the next few tokens are strongly constrained together. The extra heads are small relative to the backbone, so the training cost is modest. One design choice we cared about was keeping the causal chain intact across the predicted positions, so the auxiliary heads actually share and reinforce the main trunk's representations instead of becoming a separate shortcut.

The second job is at inference, and this is where it gets practical. Those same MTP heads give you a built-in draft model for speculative decoding. Instead of generating one token per forward pass, you propose several and verify them in one step. Because the draft comes from the model itself, the acceptance rate is high, and you get a real speedup in throughput without changing output quality. That matters a lot for serving cost. Training-side gains are nice, but inference is where most of the compute is spent over a model's lifetime.

I'd also say what MTP is not. It's not a replacement for scale or data quality, and it won't fix a weak base model. It's a relatively cheap lever that tightens representations during training and then pays you back a second time at serving. That's rare in this field, where most techniques help one side at the expense of the other. So we think of it less as a trick and more as a default component we'd want in any serious pretraining recipe going forward.

r001.rationale: The response says MTP was added in pretraining to strengthen longer-horizon representations and improve downstream benchmark performance.

r002.rationale: It describes using MTP heads for speculative decoding and faster inference, but does not say this exploits compute headroom naturally left by the model architecture.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate MTP—multi-token prediction—into two roles. During pretraining, it gives the model a richer learning signal: instead of predicting only the next token, it also learns to anticipate tokens further ahead. The intuition is that this encourages representations that are useful beyond the immediate next step, although the benefit depends on how you balance that objective with standard next-token prediction.

During inference, MTP can support speculative decoding. It proposes several tokens, and the main model verifies them, potentially letting us advance multiple tokens in a single verification pass. The actual speedup depends on acceptance rates and the overhead of proposing and checking those tokens.

So I see the two benefits as related but distinct: better learning during training, and potentially more efficient decoding at inference. You can retain the training benefit even if you don’t use the extra prediction heads when serving the model.

r001.rationale: The response describes a richer training signal and a possible training benefit, but does not clearly identify improved base-model capability as the reason Luo’s team added MTP.

r002.rationale: The response discusses speculative decoding and possible speedups, but does not explain that MTP uses compute headroom left by the model architecture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of multi-token prediction, or MTP, as serving two purposes. During pretraining, it gives the model a richer learning signal: instead of only predicting the next token, it also learns to predict further ahead. That encourages the representations to capture information that will be useful across several upcoming tokens.

During inference, those prediction modules can be used for speculative decoding. They propose additional tokens, and the main model verifies them, so we can potentially generate several tokens in one pass. The speedup depends on how often those proposals are accepted and the overhead of verification.

So I would separate the two benefits: MTP can improve training even if you don’t use the additional prediction modules at inference, and it also provides a way to accelerate inference when the serving setup supports it.
